Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2025-10-15 16:00 UTC
- Duration: ~47 minutes
- Attendees: Jamie Lin (Redwood AE), Aisha Patel (Redwood SE), Dr. Marcus Yu (CTO), Priya Anand (ML Eng), Samir Rao (Security)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
Redwood walked Orion Health through JSON-mode structured output and a tool-calling flow. Focus on schema enforcement, guardrails, and how the Console/Optimize suggestions reduce token cost and latency. Customer raised data residency and KMS/SAML questions. Agreed next steps: security pack, trial reservation, benchmark session.

Topics: structured JSON output; function/tool calling; schemas & validators; Console demo (routes, per-route SLOs); Optimize suggestions (batching/caching/quantization); security (KMS, SOC2); pilot plan.

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Jamie Lin: Hey everybody, thanks for joining, this is Jamie from Redwood, and I'm with Aisha our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:00:07] Dr. Marcus Yu: Doing well, Jamie. Thanks. We wanted to see how Redwood handles structured responses and some of the guardrail patterns, especially for EHR extraction workflows.
[00:00:18] Aisha Patel: Awesome, that's exactly what we prepared. Quick agenda: we'll do a short high-level then jump into Console and the API — JSON mode, show schemas, a tool-calling demo (think of it as the LLM calling a service to fetch patient metadata), and then Optimize suggestions.
[00:00:34] Priya Anand: Quick note — latency is sensitive for our triage UI, but costs are also a concern. We'll probably be comparing hosted vs dedicated.
[00:00:42] Jamie Lin: Totally expected. We'll show how you can pin low-latency models on Dedicated and fall back to hosted, and how Optimize gives batching/caching recommendations so you don't overspend.
[00:00:51] Samir Rao: And I'll jump in on security questions later — SAML, KMS, audit logs.

[00:01:10] Aisha Patel: Ok jumping in — here's the Console. I'm sharing a sample API route called /ehr-extract-json. In JSON mode we supply a schema — in this demo we use a strict patient-summary schema with typed fields, arrays for medications, and an enum for severity. The runtime will validate and reject or return a structured parse.
[00:01:35] Aisha Patel: NOTE: transcription sometimes reads 'Redwood Privatee' when I said 'Redwood Private', so ignore that.
[00:01:45] Priya Anand: Can the schema enforce value ranges? For example severity 1-5 only?
[00:01:52] Aisha Patel: Yes, you can declare ranges and types in the schema. We use JSON Schema style constraints and a runtime validator. If the model attempts to hallucinate an out-of-range value, the call will either fail validation or we can auto-correct with the validator strategy you choose.
[00:02:08] Dr. Marcus Yu: How often does that validator trigger? We're worried about retries increasing latency.
[00:02:14] Aisha Patel: Good question. By default it's post-generation validation — quick check. For high-sensitivity routes you can enable constrained decoding (nucleus + token filters) and a fallback to a safer model variant. For Dedicated low-latency SLOs we recommend combining constrained decoding with prefix caching — that keeps most calls within SLO.
[00:02:34] Jamie Lin: I'll also add that Optimize will show a prediction of added latency for each setting change so you can quantify it before applying.

[00:02:46] Jamie Lin: Now the tool-calling demo: we have a small mock 'patient-metadata' service that the model can call to fetch demographics and consent flags. Watch the flow — prompt -> model emits function call -> Redwood routes to the tool -> tool returns JSON -> model finishes structured output.
[00:03:06] [00:03:06] Aisha Patel: (typing) Kicking off the call — here model suggests getPatient(pid=12345). You'll see in the Console trace the exact function schema and payload.
[00:03:18] Priya Anand: Is that calling out over the public internet? For private deployments we need those tool hooks to be inside the VPC.
[00:03:26] Aisha Patel: Absolutely — for Redwood Private you can register internal webhooks over your VPC or use the on-prem package. The control plane still surfaces traces, but the traffic never leaves your network if you choose that setup.
[00:03:38] Samir Rao: What about auth on those tool endpoints? We need mTLS and token rotation.
[00:03:43] Aisha Patel: We support mTLS, bearer tokens, and can integrate with customer KMS for signing. We'll include the recommended auth patterns in the security pack.

[00:03:58] Jamie Lin: Jumping back to structured output — here's a failure case: model returns free text where we expect an array. Watch how the runtime applies the schema and then either rejects or attempts a best-effort map with reason codes.
[00:04:12] [00:04:12] Aisha Patel: See the 'validation_reason' field in the trace — the model output was coerced into the array and we marked it with a tag so downstream systems can decide to surface or ignore it.
[00:04:23] Dr. Marcus Yu: That's useful. We can't have silent corruptions. Need an explicit flag.
[00:04:27] Jamie Lin: Exactly — we surface the validation metadata so your pipeline can enforce strictness.

[00:04:40] Priya Anand: Let's talk about token usage: the schemas look verbose. Do we pay for that?
[00:04:47] Jamie Lin: Schemas are part of the prompt overhead, yes. But Optimize suggests a minimal serialized form and caching prefixes to reduce repeated schema tokens. Also server-side schema caching can avoid sending the full schema every request if you pin it to the route.
[00:05:00] Priya Anand: Pinning sounds good — can we update a pinned schema without dropping traffic?
[00:05:06] Aisha Patel: We have staged rollout (canary) for route config changes. You can push a new schema as a canary percent and monitor validation regressions. If it fails, rollback automatically.

[00:05:22] Jamie Lin: Now showing Optimize panel — it scanned historical calls and suggests reducing max_tokens for this route, enable prefix caching on a 200ms window, and quantize the model to int8 for non-critical routes. These are estimated to cut per-token cost by ~30% while keeping latency within SLA for 99th percentile.
[00:05:43] Samir Rao: Quantization — any model compatibility issues? For our EHR parsers we need numeric fidelity.
[00:05:49] Aisha Patel: We provide model-compat recommendations. Optimize will flag models where int8 might impact accuracy and offer a smaller batch/FP16 fallback for those requests. We can also run a quick eval on your prompt set to measure regression.

[00:06:05] [00:06:05] Priya Anand: Can we see a live example of function calling returning data and being merged into the structured response?
[00:06:11] Aisha Patel: Sure — demo now: model calls getPatient — tool returns {"patient_id": "12345", "consent": "yes", "last_visit": "2025-09-26"} — model completes final JSON with medications array and a recommended triage code.
[00:06:29] Dr. Marcus Yu: That triage code — can we map it to our internal ontology?
[00:06:33] Aisha Patel: Yes, you can provide a mapping table or pass an ontology file to the runtime; we support deterministic mapping post-processing or have the model output a canonical code.

[00:06:45] Jamie Lin: Quick show of the tracing view — every request has a timeline: request received, model choice, function call timestamps, validator pass/fail, and final output. You get token-level cost breakdown too.
[00:06:58] Priya Anand: Great for debugging.

[00:07:10] [00:07:10] Samir Rao: Security — we need to ensure audit logs are immutable and retained 7 years. Does Redwood support that?
[00:07:17] Jamie Lin: For private deployments you control retention; for hosted we offer add-on long-retention storage with WORM options. We'll include details in the pack.
[00:07:27] Samir Rao: SSO?
[00:07:29] Jamie Lin: SAML/SCIM yes, we integrate with IdPs. Role-based access and per-route RBAC are available.

[00:07:40] Priya Anand: About error handling — if the function endpoint times out, can Redwood retry the model with a fallback response? We can't block the UI.
[00:07:48] Aisha Patel: You can configure automatic fallback policies: default fallback text, cached last-known good response, or reroute to a cheaper model. There are circuit-breaker policies per-route.

[00:08:05] [00:08:05] Jamie Lin: Here's a small exercise — running a batch of 50 small triage requests. Watch how batching squeezes throughput and how Optimize suggests a batching window to balance latency.
[00:08:17] Aisha Patel: (notes) In the trace you can see a 50ms batching window aggregated 16 requests per batch — net cost down 22%, median latency still within target.
[00:08:30] Dr. Marcus Yu: For production we'd want guaranteed throughput — can Dedicated be configured with reserved concurrency?
[00:08:36] Jamie Lin: Yes, Dedicated is reserved capacity with autoscaling policies you can lock down. You can also reserve burst capacity for peak times.

[00:08:48] Priya Anand: Any limitations around VPC peering for the control plane? We use a private network and have vendor connections limited.
[00:08:55] Aisha Patel: For private on-prem we can air-gap control plane telemetry; for VPC we do peering and private endpoints. We'll include network diagrams in the security pack.

[00:09:10] [00:09:10] Jamie Lin: Ok taking a few quick live questions from Marcus and Priya.
[00:09:15] Dr. Marcus Yu: If we run a pilot, what's a realistic timeline?
[00:09:18] Jamie Lin: We typically do a 2–4 week pilot: week 1 onboarding & schema design, week 2 run benchmarks and Optimize tuning, week 3 iterate on regressions, week 4 handover or scale. We'll tailor it to your calendar.
[00:09:33] Priya Anand: Can we bring our own models? We have a fine-tuned model that we want to keep inside our VPC.
[00:09:39] Aisha Patel: Yes, Redwood Private supports customer-managed models. You can register a model artifact and the runtime will load it on your Dedicated nodes.

[00:09:51] Samir Rao: Compliance — do you have pen test reports we can share with InfoSec?
[00:09:55] Jamie Lin: Yes, we'll include the latest pentest report and SOC2 Type II in the security pack.

[00:10:05] [00:10:05] Aisha Patel: Wrapping up the demo portion — to summarize the guardrails: schema validation, constrained decoding, function-calling auditing, and post-processing mappings.
[00:10:15] Aisha Patel: Also note: sometimes the auto-transcript may show minor word swaps — for example 'KV cache' might appear as 'K V cash'.

[00:10:26] Jamie Lin: Next steps and proposed pilot: we'll reserve a 2-week Dedicated trial with a small GPU pool, run your triage prompt set, and produce a baseline Optimize report. We'll schedule benchmark session on 2025-10-27.
[00:10:40] Dr. Marcus Yu: Sounds good. We'll confirm internal stakeholders and provide compliance checklist.

[00:10:48] Priya Anand: One more technical question — do you support function-level RBAC? So only certain roles can call patient-export endpoints.
[00:10:56] Aisha Patel: Yes: per-route and per-function RBAC mapped to your IdP groups.

[00:11:06] [00:11:06] Jamie Lin: Great, thanks everyone. Final recap of action items in the console notes.
[00:11:12] (longer Q&A and clarifications continue; transcription clipped for brevity)
